items.longBusinessSummary: Hewlett Packard Enterprise Company, together with its subsidiaries, develops intelligent solutions in the United States, the Americas, Europe, the Middle East, Africa, the Asia Pacific, Japan, and internationally. It operates in five segments: Server, Hybrid Cloud, Networking, Financial Services, and Corporate Investments and Other. The company offers general-purpose servers, workload-optimized servers, and integrated systems, including HPE ProLiant Rack and Tower servers; HPE Synergy; HPE Scale Up servers; HPE Edgeline servers; HPE Cray EX; HPE Cray XD; and HPE NonStop. It also provides cloud-native and hybrid solutions, such as HPE Alletra Storage; HPE InfoSight; HPE CloudPhysics; and HPE GreenLake. In addition, the company develops and sells networking and security products and services comprising hardware products, which include Wi-Fi and private cellular access points, MX and PTX routers, and gateways, as well as QFX, EX, and CX switches; software products, such as Mist and Aruba Central; and services comprising professional, maintenance, support services, management software, and education and training programs. Further, it offers investment solutions, including leasing, financing, IT consumption, utility programs, and asset management services, as well as supports financial solutions for on-premise flexible consumption models. The company serves commercial and large enterprise groups, as well as business and public sector enterprises. It sells its products through resellers, distribution partners, master area partners, original equipment manufacturers, independent software vendors, systems integrators, and advisory firms. The company was founded in 1939 and is headquartered in Spring, Texas.

667358459,Carruthers_G_Willikins,"$SMCI $DELL $HPE $NVDA $MU You're oversimplifying the differences between these business models. Dell's customer financing does introduce credit risk, but much of that exposure is managed through structured financing and securitisation arrangements. HPE similarly offers customer financing through HPE Financial Services, without that automatically making its business model inherently riskier. Both Dell and HPE also benefit from established supplier relationships, purchasing scale and financing arrangements. Meanwhile, SMCI's approach of committing substantial capital upfront creates significant liquidity, inventory and working-capital risks of its own. You're also attributing Dell's share-price weakness specifically to supply-chain and financing concerns without demonstrating that connection. There's simply no evidence that SMCI's operating model makes it substantially less risky than Dell's or HPE's. You're confusing different ways of managing risk with the elimination of risk.",2026-10-26T14:42:05Z,3,neutral

667358176,Carruthers_G_Willikins,"$SMCI $DELL $HPE $NVDA $MU There's some truth to this, but you're confusing reducing a supplier's risk with reducing $SMCI's own risk. Paying suppliers promptly can certainly improve relationships and potentially secure better allocation, but it also shifts significant financial exposure onto SMCI itself. At the end of FY2026, the company was carrying $12.9 billion in inventory and had $34.2 billion in non-cancellable purchase commitments, while a single supplier accounted for 63.1% of its purchases. That's substantial inventory, working-capital and supplier concentration risk. More importantly, there's no evidence that SMCI actually receives preferential allocation compared with competitors like $DELL or $HPE. So while the underlying procurement argument is reasonable, presenting it as evidence that SMCI is a safer investment is a considerable leap that the available data simply doesn't support.",2026-10-26T14:40:12Z,1,positive

Title: CloudCasa Expands Disaster Recovery Integrations with Enterprise Storage Vendors and Introduces a Model Context Protocol Server for AI Tools
Author: CloudCasa by Catalogic   Tue, October 27, 2026 at 1:02 PM GMT+1 2 min read
Published: 2026-10-27T12:02:00+00:00
=== BODY ===
Latest CloudCasa update adds a preview of backups using Changed Block Tracking
Paramus, NJ, Oct. 27, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- CloudCasa by Catalogic today announced its latest feature update, led by CloudCasa Disaster Recovery (DR) support for an additional enterprise array, new Model Context Protocol (MCP) support that allows agents and AI tools to interact with CloudCasa, and a preview of Changed Block Tracking (CBT) support for virtual machine backups.
Storage-Integrated Disaster Recovery. Dell PowerStore now joins HPE Alletra Storage MP B10000, HPE Alletra 9000, and SUSE Storage as supported storage replication providers for CloudCasa DR. With CloudCasa DR, the storage system replicates persistent volume data to the recovery site, while CloudCasa orchestrates DR failover and failback of Kubernetes applications and KubeVirt VMs. Details are available for Dell PowerStore and HPE Alletra.
Model Context Protocol (MCP) Support. CloudCasa now provides an MCP server, enabling AI agents to easily access and interact with CloudCasa's capabilities. Platform teams can now monitor and report on their data protection and DR status using agents and other AI tools compatible with MCP.
Changed Block Tracking Preview. CloudCasa has added support for virtual machine backups using CBT, to significantly shorten backup times. CBT identifies and logs which specific disk blocks have been modified since a previous backup.
"Platform teams do more of their day-to-day work using AI assistants, and they want backup status available alongside the rest of their tooling," said Ryan Kaw, Global VP of Sales and Alliances at CloudCasa. "The MCP server makes that possible today. This latest update to CloudCasa ensures that our clients can depend on us making virtual machine data protection faster and more efficient."
The updated CloudCasa feature set is available now with CBT backups in preview. Full details are in the latest CloudCasa release notes.
CloudCasa, powered by Catalogic Software, delivers cloud-native backup and disaster recovery designed specifically for Kubernetes and modern application environments. The platform provides automated protection, granular recovery, migration, and ransomware resilience to help organizations safeguard applications and data across public cloud, private cloud, hybrid, and edge infrastructures. Trusted by enterprises and service providers worldwide, CloudCasa helps simplify data protection while supporting operational consistency at scale. Learn more at cloudcasa.io.
Dell and PowerStore are trademarks of Dell Inc. or its subsidiaries. HPE and Alletra are trademarks of Hewlett Packard Enterprise Development LP. SUSE is a registered trademark of SUSE LLC in the United States and other countries. All other trademarks are the property of their respective owners.

Title: Would You Have Held NetApp Stock All The Way Up?
Author: Trefis Team   Tue, October 27, 2026 at 11:26 AM GMT+1 3 min read
Published: 2026-10-27T10:26:08+00:00
=== BODY ===
For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com.
A $10,000 investment in NetApp (NTAP) stock grew to $65,318 over the past ten years before dividends. The same capital in the S&P 500 reached $35,820. In hindsight, deciding to buy looks like the only question, but the harder test was holding on. How many times do you think NetApp stock fell 20% or more on the way up?
Over the past ten years, NetApp stock fell 20% or more three times, with each decline ultimately exceeding 30%.
The deepest drop stretched from September 2018 to March 2020, a period when the stock lost 59.8% and the S&P 500 fell 22.8%. Shareholders then waited another 17.2 months after that low until August 2021 before NetApp again closed above its September 2018 high.
What Did Holding NetApp Through A Fall Feel Like?
The most recent downturn began in July 2024 and lasted 8.8 months. At the April 2025 low, the position was down 43.5%. The stock then took another 13.6 months, until May 2026, to finally close above its July 2024 high.
Every one of NetApp's declines eventually ended. Yet an investor holding shares at the April 2025 low had no way to know that this drop would reverse, or when.
Was Something Wrong With NetApp's Business?
NetApp's twelve-month revenue fell during only one of the three stock declines, which was the deepest. The company sells data storage primarily through its Hybrid Cloud business, a segment accounting for 90.1% of revenue in fiscal 2026. The rest came from Public Cloud, encompassing storage services sold in the public cloud.
During that deepest drop, twelve-month revenue was 7.7% lower at the March 2020 low than at the September 2018 high. The operating margin barely shifted over the same period, edging from 17.7% to 17.2%. The business weakened only slightly, yet the stock dropped far more than revenue did.
The 2024 downturn unfolded differently. Twelve-month revenue at the April 2025 low was 3.8% higher than at the July 2024 high, and the operating margin climbed from 20.2% to 21.5%. The business remained solid by both measures, so the 43.5% drop did not come from weaker revenue or margins.
What Selling NetApp Stock Would Have Cost
NetApp stock has gained 528.2% since its March 2020 low, and anyone who sold at the bottom missed the entire rally. Today, the shares trade 7.1% below the highest close of the ten years, which occurred on October 12, 2026.
These severe drops served as the cost of admission for NetApp's overall gain, and only investors who sat through all three captured the full ten-year return. The next time NetApp stock drops sharply, compare the decline against its twelve-month revenue. In the 2018 to 2020 downturn, the stock fell far more than revenue did. In the 2024 decline, revenue actually grew. Both times, the stock eventually closed above its prior high.
Is Too Much Of Your Wealth Riding On One Stock?
NetApp holders who stayed for the gain also sat through the falls. When one position grows into a large part of your wealth, a sharp fall can hurt your whole plan, and selling to spread the money out can bring a large tax bill.
